title: The Tale of Melon City
subject: English

notes.heading: Theme
notes.text: The poem sharply satirizes arbitrary governance, blind adherence to tradition, and the absurdity of a purely mechanical legal system where citizens value complete peace and non-interference over the logical capabilities of their leader.

summary: "The Tale of Melon City" by Vikram Seth is a humorous, narrative poem that sharply satirizes arbitrary governance, blind adherence to tradition, and the absurdity of a purely mechanical legal system. The story begins with a description of a "just and placid" King who rules over an ancient state and proclaims that a magnificent archway be constructed across the main thoroughfare to morally and aesthetically uplift the spectators. However, when the King proudly rides under the newly completed structure, his crown strikes the low arch and falls off. Interpreting this accident as a monumental disgrace to his royal honor, the furious King immediately demands that the chief of builders be hanged. This spark triggers a comical and farcical chain of blame-shifting within the kingdom: the chief builder shifts the fault to the labourers; the labourers blame the masons for using wrong-sized bricks; the masons blame the architect; and the architect cleverly implicates the King himself by reminding him that he had altered the original blueprints. Perplexed by this reversal, the King seeks counsel from the "wisest man" in the kingdom, an old, blind sage who foolishly decrees that since the arch struck the crown, the arch itself must be hanged. However, a councillor objects, arguing that it would be a shameful sin to execute an object that has touched the royal head. As the process stalls, the gathered mob grows restless and bloodthirsty for a public execution. Fearing a popular rebellion, the King compromises by ordering that whoever fits the hanging noose perfectly will be executed. One by one, every person is measured, but the noose hangs so high that the only person tall enough to fit it is the King himself. In full accordance with his own absolute decree, the King is promptly hanged. Left without a monarch, the ministers execute an absurd custom dictating that the very next person who walks through the city gates will choose their new ruler. The individual turns out to be an idiot who, when questioned, responds with his favorite standard answer: "A melon". Adhering strictly to tradition without applying any logic, the ministers ceremoniously crown a melon as their new King. Years pass, and the citizens remain perfectly content with their silent, non-interfering ruler, valuing complete laissez-faire and peace over the identity of their monarch, illustrating the sheer irony of public reasoning.

qa.q: Narrate “The Tale of Melon City” in your own words.
qa.a: The poem tells the humorous story of a foolish king who wants his people to have a peaceful and happy life. One day, an arch is built too low and knocks off his crown. The king orders the guilty person to be hanged, but the blame keeps passing from one person to another. Finally, the king himself is found guilty and is hanged. According to an old custom, the next person to pass the noose is made king, and a melon becomes the new king. The people accept this without question and continue living peacefully.

qa.q: What impression do you form of the king from the poem?
qa.a: The king appears foolish, unreasonable and careless. He wants to be known as a just ruler but makes decisions without thinking. He changes his orders repeatedly and finally becomes a victim of his own foolish system. The poet uses humour to show the absurdity of such leadership.

qa.q: What is the significance of the melon becoming the king?
qa.a: The melon becoming the king is humorous and ironic. It shows how meaningless the system of choosing a ruler has become. The people do not care who rules them as long as they are left in peace. It also highlights the poet’s criticism of blind obedience and foolish governance.

qa.q: What message does the poem convey?
qa.a: The poem conveys that a government based on foolish decisions and blind obedience can become absurd. It also shows that people sometimes accept poor leadership without questioning it, as long as their daily lives remain peaceful. The poem presents these ideas through satire and humour.
